measures.what_it_does: Authorizes a three-year South Kitsap School District capital levy (2027-2029) for elementary security cameras, intercoms, entrance access controls and bus radios, student Chromebooks and cybersecurity, a high school theater renovation and gym bleachers, and synthetic turf fields at South Kitsap High and Marcus Whitman Middle School. Passes with a simple majority.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value: $23.5 million (2027), $24.2 million (2028) and $24.9 million (2029), $72.6 million in total. That is about $750 a year on a $500,000 home (the district rounds to $756). It is not described as replacing an expiring levy and would be collected alongside the district's EP&O levy.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Katherine Ander and Carl Olson, South Kitsap School Supporters) says the state does not pay for most school repairs or technology, and that even the newest schools are over 30 years old. It says the money must stay in South Kitsap for voter-approved projects, and acting now avoids costlier failures later.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed. The Auditor's Office recruited by text, email, press release and social media, and no one came forward.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new three-year property tax of about $1.50 per $1,000 ($72.6 million). No source describes it as replacing an expiring levy, and the district has no bond debt. Whether any of the 2018 capital levy is still being collected was not found; if it were, that would argue for +1.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7380 (S1); the district's levy page and flyer (S2-S3); South Kitsap School Supporters (S4); Kitsap Daily News / Port Orchard Independent coverage of the 2026 levy (S5-S6), the 2018 capital levy (S7), the district's 2024 plans after the failed bond (S8), and the 2026 campaign (S9). A Kitsap Sun story was paywalled (HTTP 402) and not used.

measures.what_it_does: Asks whether Kitsap Public Utility District (KPUD), now a water, wastewater and fiber utility, may build or buy electric generation, transmission or distribution facilities. Puget Sound Energy serves the county today. A yes vote gives KPUD that authority permanently with no second public vote required, though it does not have to use it. The board has committed to a feasibility study first, and if PSE will not sell, KPUD could seek to acquire the system through condemnation. A no vote ends the current effort.
measures.cost_line: No tax, rate or bond in the ballot title. KPUD says property taxes and rates would not change because of the vote. A yes vote does trigger the board's promised feasibility study, estimated at $300,000-$500,000. The cost of any later acquisition is unknown; Jefferson PUD paid $103 million for PSE's much smaller Jefferson County system in 2010.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (David Behar, William Woznicki and Sue Ellen White) says a yes vote allows a transparent study of public power, and the effort stops if the numbers don't work. It argues PUD rates run below PSE's, that money paid to PSE shareholders could stay local, and that decisions would be closer to ratepayers.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Varon Mullis, Robert P. McGee and Shannon Turner, Citizens for Accountable Utilities in Kitsap) says the measure grants broad, permanent authority to buy or build a utility before any cost evidence, with no second vote. It notes that similar measures failed in Skagit, Island and Thurston counties, and that KPUD can study costs without this vote.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7376 (S1); KPUD's Exploring Electric Service page, Prop 1 fact publication, Resolution 26-07-28A, the June 22, 2026 general manager memo, an Oct. 7 presentation and a July listening-session post (S2-S7); Kitsap Daily News coverage including PSE's response (S8); RCW 54.08.070 and 54.16.040 (S9-S10). No lean: the measure raises no tax and authorizes no spending, and the local-control reading (state-regulated private utility versus locally governed public one) does not fit the rubric's poles. Kitsap Sun stories were paywalled (HTTP 402) and not used.
